newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria wants France to keep out of its affairs.
newsitem.headline: Algeria wants France to keep out of its affairs.

text.p: Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf, reacting to French officials' comments, said on Friday that France should keep out of Algeria's internal affairs.

"We have never asked for France's support but on the contrary...Algeria wishes that France should not interfere in our affairs. This is what I have repeated to French leaders each time I have had the occasion to meet them," Attaf told Algerian radio Chaine III.
"I insisted on the fact that our relations should be based on mutual respect, which means non-interference, balance of interests and dialogue," Attaf said.

The French weekly l'Express reported on Thursday French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette commenting on the recent wave of violence in Algeria in which union leader Abdelhak Benhamouda was assassinated said:
"Algeria is not France. That must be understood and admitted once and for all. It is a sovereign country."
"It is up to Algeria to solve its problems, up to the Algerian people to decide their destiny," he said.

Ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, head of the National Assembly's Foreign Affairs Committee, summed up French policy after de Charette briefed a special closed-door session of the panel on Algeria as "neither intervention nor interference".
He stressed that Paris, which suffered a wave of bombings in 1995 blamed on Algerian rebels and which faces threats of fresh attacks, wanted to be in step with its European Union partners.
But the former French president also called for a dialogue between Algerian authorities and the outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) in order to end five years of political violence.
"Giscard d'Estaing is far away from Algeria's realities...His statement is an unhealthy contribution to the rehabilitation of those who were behind the present Algerian tragedy," Attaf added.
He said Italy's ambassador to Algeria had been summoned to the foreign ministry over a senior Italian official's remarks in the Italian newspaper Unita.
Italian foreign undersecretary Piero Fassino was quoted as saying Italy planned to present a peace proposal on Algeria at a meeting of foreign ministers of Italy, Spain and France on February 3.

Attaf said Algiers' envoy to Rome had met the Italian secretaries of state and been assured there was no Italian initiative on the North African country, that Italy barred itself from any interference in Algerian internal affairs, and that Rome's aim was to help isolate "terrorism" on the international level.

An estimated 60,000 people have been killed since Algeria plunged into civil strife after the authorities cancelled 1992 elections that FIS was poised to win. A surge of violence has flared up during the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan which started on January 10. More than 170 people have died since then.
